To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) G93 is a critical player in Na+/I- stoichiometric coupling, anion selectivity, and electrogenicity of NIS; 2) the longer the side chains at position 93 the higher the Km and lower the Vmax for the anion substrate; and 3) a 3D homolgy model of NIS, based on the structure bacterial Na+ galactose transporter, identifies G93 as the pivot of the transporter.
the G93 position in NIS is critical in the anion binding pocket and in determining the anion selectivity of the transporter, and that G93 plays a key role in the mechanism of Na+/I- transport.

the G93R mutation causes congenital I- uptake defect, that the side chain length at position 93 is important for anion selectivity, that G93 is a key player in the mechanism, and that the NIS mechanism is electrogenic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the mechanism of anion selectivities and stoichiometry in the NIS.
the mechanism of the Na+/anion symport and its clinical relevance, and has led to the discovery of a novel anion-selective NIS mutant.
the molecular mechanism and the regulation of the sodium-dependent iodide transporter (NIS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
G93R is a loss-of-function mutant, and the other mutants have a gain-of-function phenotype.
the G93R mutation, in addition to its role in the mechanism of I- transport, plays a critical role in the mechanism that determines the anion selectivity of the transporter.
the Na+/I-symporter (NIS), the first step of the thyroid hormone biosynthetic pathway, mediates the electrogenic 2∶ 1 stoichiometry Na+/I- cotransport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
G93 is a key determinant of the Na+/anion stoichiometry, anion specificity, and the transport mechanism of NIS.

the G93 residue of NIS plays a critical role in the mechanism of NIS, and that the anion-binding site of NIS is formed by residues in the extracellular loop II, and that the selectivity filter is located at the cytosolic end of the loop.

the G93R mutation, which abolishes I- transport, causes a change in the conformation of the NIS that results in a 2Na+∶1I- stoichometry, and that the G93E/Q mutations, which cause anion discrimination, result in an inwardly open state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NIS mechanism is different from that of other Na+-dependent transporters.

NIS, and likely other members of the SLC5 family of transporters, are electrogenic and that the anion binding pocket in NIS is located on the cytoplasmic side of the protein, a feature that may be common to other members of this transporter family.
G93 is a key player in anion recognition, anion selectivity, and anion stoichiometry of NIS.
